title: Housing pigs through winter
subtitle: Deep straw, a draught-free arc, and dry ground are all pigs actually need. Getting any of those wrong costs you sleep.
excerpt: Pigs do not thermoregulate as efficiently as sheep or cattle in cold wet conditions. A pig sleeping on wet ground in a draughty ark will lose condition fast regardless of how much it is fed. Deep straw management keeps the bed dry and warm from below; the arc keeps wind and rain out from above.
sourceNotes: DEFRA Codes of Recommendations for the Welfare of Pigs, outdoor housing section. AHDB Pork smallholding management notes. John Seymour, The New Complete Book of Self-Sufficiency (2003), chapter on pigs. Carla Emery, Encyclopedia of Country Living (1994), winter pig management section.

glossaryTerms.definition: A curved galvanised steel shelter, open at one end, used as outdoor pig housing. The curved roof sheds rain and provides an enclosed sleeping area. Typically 1.8–2.4 m long and 1.2–1.5 m wide.

A bedding system in which straw is added on top of existing bedding rather than fully removed each day. Decomposition of the lower layers generates warmth from below. Requires mucking out every 2–4 weeks when ammonia builds up.

content.text: with dry ground beneath it come through a UK winter comfortably. The challenge is usually the ground, not the weather: a November field that looked dry in September can become a quagmire of mud and standing water that exposes the arc floor to damp from below.

Before conditions deteriorate, move the arc to the highest, driest corner of the paddock. Face the open end away from the prevailing wind, in the UK, typically away from the south-west. If the ground is clay-heavy, lay a hardcore base of road planings or a timber pallet under the arc before it sinks in.

Restrict the pigs' access to the rest of the field using electric tape. Concentrating activity near the arc in a smaller area gives the rest of the field a chance to recover and keeps the area around the arc from becoming waterlogged too quickly.
Start with a base layer of 20-25 cm of straw at the beginning of winter. Add 5-8 cm of fresh straw daily or every other day on top of what is already there. This is
: the base decomposes and generates warmth from below. Pigs sleeping on a deep straw bed are insulated from the cold arc floor even when air temperature drops.
Smell the arc each morning. A strong ammonia smell indicates the lower layers have composted beyond the useful stage and the whole bed needs mucking out.
On a dry day every 2-4 weeks, muck out completely: remove all straw, scrape the arc floor, air it for two hours, then relay from scratch.
Pigs will push wet straw toward the arc entrance. Remove the damp front layer separately and push dry straw forward to replace it.

Pigs drink 5-10 litres of water per day and will stop eating if water is unavailable. Standard nipple drinkers freeze at -1°C. Options: a heated drinker (a worthwhile investment if you run pigs through winter regularly), filling a rubber trough with warm water twice daily, or using an insulated trough with a foam jacket.

Check the drinker first thing every morning before feeding. A pig that has been without water overnight and then receives a full ration may develop salt poisoning if the feed contains normal salt levels and the gut is dehydrated. Vet call if a pig staggers, presses its head against objects, or shows aimless circling after a period without water.

Pigs burn more energy keeping warm in cold weather. Increase the daily ration by 10-15% from November through February, checking body condition fortnightly. A pig going into autumn at the right condition needs this adjustment to maintain it through the cold months.
